title: The turban in court
hook: Sikh families win cases in several countries to wear the turban at school and work

segments.voice: Yesterday, parkash: foundries, mill towns, and your line, a house became a gurdwara. Today, from one of those British towns, a schoolboy's turban goes all the way to the highest court in the land.

Birmingham, the late 1970s. A father takes his son to a private school to enroll him. The boy is a Sikh, with uncut hair tied up under a small turban. The headmaster is polite, and firm: the boy can come, but the turban must go, and the hair must be cut, to match the school uniform. The father says no. That could have been the end of it: find another school, move on. Instead, the family went to court.
screen: `BIRMINGHAM, THE LATE 1970S.` → `THE TURBAN MUST GO.` → `THE FATHER SAYS NO.`

segments.voice: Why it matters: for many Sikhs, uncut hair, kesh, is a gift to be kept as God made it, and the turban, the dastar, covers and honors it. It is not a hat you take off to be polite. Sikh tradition says Guru Gobind Singh made uncut hair one of the marks of the Khalsa, and for many Sikhs, being told to remove the turban in public is like being told to set aside part of who they are. The boy was Gurinder Singh Mandla. His family lost in the first courts: the appeal judges said Sikhs were a religious group, not a racial one, so the race discrimination law didn't cover them. The family kept going. In 1983 the House of Lords, then Britain's highest court, ruled for them. Sikhs, it said, are a community with a long shared history and culture of their own, an ethnic group under the law, and the school had discriminated. Lawyers still use the test the Lords set out. The question came up beyond the courtroom too. In Britain, Sikh bus drivers campaigned to wear the turban on the job, and won. In Canada, the national police changed its rules in 1990, and Baltej Singh Dhillon joined wearing a turban; later court challenges to the change failed. In the United States, after lawsuits and long campaigns, the Army now lets Sikh soldiers serve with turbans and beards. Each time, a family or a single person said: I can do this job, and learn in this school, and still be myself.
screen: `KESH AND THE DASTAR.` · `MANDLA: LOSING, THEN WINNING, 1983.` · `BUS DRIVERS, POLICE, SOLDIERS.` · `DO THE JOB, STAY YOURSELF.` · then, large: `THE RIGHT TO BE YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Think of the head coverings you see: a turban, a patka, a hijab, a kippah, a nun's veil, a headscarf, a cap. Picture one person you've seen wearing one, and imagine what it means to them: a promise, a memory, a way of standing before God, a family. Let curiosity replace any quick judgment.
Dastar. The turban — Sikh families and workers won cases in Britain, Canada and the United States for the right to wear it at school and at work.
Your line: the right to be yourself. One schoolboy's turban still shapes British law. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs keep uncut hair (kesh) and wear a turban (dastar) every day, and Sikh organizations help families and workers who are asked to remove it at school or work.
